tests_note: The suite was never run for this table. Every row comes from reading the test files, so every row is a reading and not a measurement. Confidence is inferred on all 35 rows.

tests.label: Adding, removing and reordering projects on the map server's landing page

tests.why: The only test that sends real requests to the server, and only for page assets and one project's view.

tests.gap: No test sends an add, a remove or a reorder request. The header check that blocks other websites is never exercised. A break there lets any page you visit rewrite your project list.

tests.label: The helper script that stamps a build and moves a map out of a project
tests.gap: Nothing runs the script. Moving is the default rather than copying. A wrong folder sends the only copy of a map somewhere unexpected. Recovery means hunting for the files by hand.

tests.label: The recent-projects list and the folder browser on the landing page

tests.why: Checks the folder listing helper marks which folders hold a map, but never through a request.

tests.gap: No test sends either request. The folder browser answers for any directory on the machine, including folders far outside every served project. A widened answer there stays invisible until a person notices.

tests.label: The landing page, a project's own page and the server's health answer

tests.why: Sends real requests for the shared page assets and for one project's view, and for nothing else.

tests.gap: No test asks for those three addresses. A break leaves the server running while no page ever loads. Only a person opening a browser would find out.

tests.label: Opening an element's line in the editor or on the code hosting site
tests.gap: Nothing exercises how the link is built or which editor schemes are allowed. A wrong link opens the wrong file, or a scheme the reader never wanted. The reader would trust a line the map does not name.

tests.label: Starting the map server, popping the browser open, and stopping on the stop key

tests.why: Records the server as the one command no test may call, because starting it takes a port.

tests.gap: The start command is deliberately never called by any test. A bad option or a failed start ships unnoticed. Every reading path begins here, so a break blocks the whole browser page.

tests.label: Folding a change report back into the map and re-pinning it to the new commit

tests.why: Checks the written instructions still name commands that exist, without ever performing the fold.

tests.gap: No test performs the fold. The step is written instructions an agent follows by hand. A wrong fold quietly loses map rows, or pins the map to the wrong commit.

tests.label: The three browser libraries that draw the diagrams, pan them and colour the code

tests.why: Checks the served page text asks for the drawing library and hands it the diagram to build.

tests.gap: No test draws a diagram in a real browser. A library upgrade that changes drawing rules passes every check here. The reader meets the broken picture first.

tests.label: How the browser page behaves when a reader clicks a box, drills in and goes back

tests.why: Parses the page's script so a broken edit cannot ship silently.
Reads the script's own text to check well over a hundred screen rules, without running the page.
Checks the served page and its script agree on what each view draws.

tests.gap: Nothing loads the page and clicks it. Almost every check reads the script as text, so a rule can be present and still not work. A reader meets the break before any test does.

tests.label: The one story column that lists every feature in the order the product runs

tests.why: Pins which use cases, rules and components each feature reaches, read from the stored map.
Checks the script text draws the story diagram on the features landing screen.

tests.gap: The join behind the column is well pinned. The drawing itself is only checked as script text. A layout break in the story column fails nothing.

tests.label: The written method, the worker briefings, and the skill copied into the coding agents

tests.why: Checks every command the written method names still exists and still takes the options named.
Checks the reason for each rule stays attached to the rule.
Checks the installed copies do not point at files that were renamed or deleted.
Checks a promised outcome and the review that reads it still point at each other.

tests.gap: The install step itself never runs in a test. Only the words inside the files are checked. A broken install leaves a coding agent that cannot answer to the product at all.

tests.label: Judges reading both maps and returning grounding and rubric verdicts

tests.why: Feeds a scripted stand-in judge, so gathering the verdicts and taking the middle score are pinned.

tests.gap: No real reader is ever asked to judge. A change to what the judges are asked, or to how their answers are read, is invisible here. A judge that quietly reads worse makes every later comparison wrong.

tests.label: The harness that plants false claims to measure how many the skeptics catch

tests.why: Eight checks over the planting step and the answer key it writes.

tests.gap: Eight checks cover a harness whose own correctness decides a published score. A planted claim that turns out to be true makes a correct skeptic look wrong. The resulting number would still be believed.

tests.label: Changing the map by asking for a split, a rename, a move or a deeper drill

tests.why: Checks the written instructions for the edit still name real commands.
Pins the gate run the edited map has to pass afterwards.

tests.gap: The edit is agent work, so no test performs one. Only the gates that follow are covered. An edit that drops rows passes whenever the gates do not look for those rows.

tests.label: Finding names in files written in languages other than Python

tests.why: Runs the sizing pass; the checks for other languages only run when the grammar pack is installed.
Pins the leaf rule that decides how coarse the map may be.

tests.gap: The checks for other languages skip themselves when the grammar pack is missing. A machine without the pack reports a green suite that proved less. A grammar upgrade that changes what counts as a name would not fail here.

tests.label: Picking up a map edited while the server runs, and warning when the tool's own code changed

tests.why: An edited map is served on the next request instead of the cached one.
A broken edit keeps the last good drawings and retries later.

tests.gap: The map freshness check is well pinned. The warning about the tool's own code changing has no test. A stale server would keep serving old drawings with no notice to the reader.

tests.label: The gate that checks a finished map is well formed before anyone trusts it

tests.why: Around three hundred checks over unresolved references, missing code links and softer advice.
Drives the gate through the real command against a committed map.

tests.gap: Nothing proves the list of checks is complete. A map defect nobody has thought of still passes. The list grows only after a defect is found in a real build.

tests.label: The gate that makes the map's two layers refute each other

tests.why: Scenario maps written in the same format the gate reads, so the live path is exercised.
Runs the gate against a small planted project and its expected map.

tests.gap: The scenarios are hand written, so a contradiction nobody imagined goes unjudged. A real map is far larger than any scenario here.

tests.label: Merging the workers' fragments into one map

tests.why: Sixty-six checks over clashing ids, dropped rows and the order rows come out in.
Merges a committed set of real fragments end to end and compares against the expected map.
Reading and writing one fragment on its own, before the merge.

tests.gap: Cover is strong for dropped rows and clashing ids, which is the risk that matters. The end to end corpus is one committed project, so an unusual fragment shape stays untried.

tests.label: Handing a worker its brief, and the worker's own check before it hands work back

tests.why: Pins that each worker gets its own half of the brief, not the whole file.
Forty-three checks over the per-fragment self-check, including invented ids.

tests.gap: The brief and the self-check are pinned as text and as exit codes. Nothing proves a worker actually reads the brief it is handed.

tests.label: The record of what the skeptics proved, and the counts the gate reads

tests.why: Fifty checks that the four counts are worked out from the verdicts, never typed by hand.
Shows, per element, what was proved beside what the author claimed.
Drives every grounding verb through the real command against a realistic map.

tests.gap: The counts are worked out rather than typed, and the working is pinned. Nothing checks that the verdict files a real skeptic writes are honest in the first place.

tests.label: Correcting a code link, dropping a refuted claim, and writing down an accepted advisory

tests.why: Over a hundred checks across the repair verbs that edit a map in place.
One reader for accepted advisories, after four separate readers each silenced more than named.
Lists every code link that has slid off the line it should point at.
Checks a code link points at a line that could really be doing the work.

tests.gap: Silencing more than was named is directly tested, which is the risk that matters most here. A repair still rewrites a committed map in place with no way back.

tests.label: The pre-commit run that puts a map through every gate at once

tests.why: Forty-six checks, and they state plainly that the run is a convenience, not an enforcement point.
Catches a security claim that vanished between two maps of unchanged code.

tests.gap: Nothing forces a build to make the run at all. A map can reach a commit with no gate ever having read it. The tests say so rather than fixing it.

tests.label: Reporting what a code change did to the map

tests.why: Named code changes replayed in real temporary projects, not imitations.
Pins how far a change spreads through the map's own relations.
Pins the reading guards, so a file outside the served project is refused.

tests.gap: Real temporary projects back the checks, which is the right shape. The code changes replayed are a fixed set, so an unusual change stays unmeasured.

tests.label: Seeing what an edit changed in the map, row by row

tests.why: Twenty-five checks, written after a count-only report cost an hour of hand reading.

tests.gap: The row by row comparison is pinned on small hand built maps. A very large map's report has never been checked for readability or for speed.

tests.label: The briefing, the ignore list, and the sizing pass that runs before any map is built

tests.why: Checks the briefing says which files will be read and what the commit pin means.
Twenty-six checks over the file that declares code the map should not describe.
Thirty checks over the sizing pass and the summary a coding agent reads back.
Pins which files the walk enumerates, since a missed file is invisible to everything after.

tests.gap: The file walk is pinned to what the project tracks, which decides everything downstream. A file the walk misses stays invisible to every later check, including the coverage ones.

tests.label: Turning path rules into an explicit list of assignments

tests.why: Fifty-two checks, written after a build reported no components while assigning four hundred.

tests.gap: The failure that prompted the command, a rule matching nothing, is pinned. Very large assignment files are covered by one committed example only.

tests.label: The map document itself, and looking up one part of it

tests.why: Saving and loading a map gives back exactly what went in, in a fixed order.
Twenty-seven checks over the fixed slices a reader can ask for.
Checks the published description of the map file still matches the map.
Guards that the deleted text format stays deleted everywhere.

tests.gap: Saving and loading round trips exactly, and the old text format stays gone. A map written by a much older release is tolerated only on the scoring side, never here.

tests.label: Reading the code under a box, at the commit the map names

tests.why: Refuses absolute paths, paths that climb out, backslashes and hidden characters.
Refuses ignored files, project internals, and a link that points outside the project.
Reads real files out of a real project at a named commit.

tests.gap: Reading outside the served project is refused several ways, which is the risk that matters. Nothing checks the coloured code the reader actually sees on screen.

tests.label: Scoring a rebuilt map against the accepted one, and accepting a run as the new baseline

tests.why: Thirty-four checks over the score, the reusable heart of the whole comparison.
Sixty-eight checks over the bands that decide the pass, drift and blocking verdicts.
The whole run end to end, with a scripted stand-in judge.
Reads a map an older release wrote, so a comparison against an archive can still run.

tests.gap: Scoring and the three verdicts are heavily pinned. The thresholds themselves are a judgement call no test can defend. A threshold set too loose passes a map that got worse.

tests.label: Reading a build transcript, scoring the build's behaviour, and reporting what it spent

tests.why: Thirty checks over reading a build transcript in slices.
Over two hundred checks over the ten behaviour assertions, on made-up turn sequences.
Twenty-four checks over what a build spent.
Runs the scorecard against eight real build transcripts, but only when switched on.

tests.gap: The run against eight real transcripts is opt in, so an ordinary run skips it. Only made-up turn sequences are checked by default, and a real build looks nothing like them.

tests.label: Refusing to review an unfinished build, and archiving a map for a fresh rebuild

tests.why: Eighteen checks aimed at not losing the map while moving it aside.
Pins the guard that spots a build still running, since the stamp is written near the end.

tests.gap: Not losing the map during an archive is directly tested. Recovering from an archive that stopped halfway is not covered anywhere.

tests.label: Building the diagrams, the graph behind them, and the file browser tree

tests.why: Over a hundred checks across the graph, the views and the diagram text.
A committed real world map is the golden case every view is measured against.
Fifty-four checks over the deployment drawing alone.
Pins how stores group, who writes them and who reads them.
Pins the file tree and the overlay showing which files the map covers.

tests.gap: A committed real world map as the golden case catches drift well. What is checked is diagram text, never a drawn picture. A diagram that describes correctly and draws badly passes.

tests.label: Re-balancing the diagrams so no box has too many or too few children

tests.why: Forty-six checks over the fan-out bands, the exemptions and the escape hatch.

tests.gap: The bands and the escape hatch are pinned. Whether those bands match what a reader finds readable is never measured. Only a person can say a diagram is too busy.

tests.label: Stamping which conversation built the map

tests.why: Thirteen checks, written after the stamp existed only in a script the product does not install.

tests.gap: Writing and reading the stamp are covered by the shipped command. The older helper script that also writes the same stamp has no test at all.

rules.statement: Version control decides which files a map may describe. A project with no version control falls back to a walk of the disk.
rules.name: Version control owns the file set

sites.why: asks version control for the files it tracks, instead of walking the disk
adds files a person created but never added, and drops everything version control is told to ignore
falls back to reading the disk when the folder is not under version control

rules.risk: Code that version control hides never reaches the map. An absent folder then reads exactly like a folder that was looked at and found empty.

rules.statement: Installed packages, build output, lock files and images are never analysed, so the map measures code people wrote.
rules.name: Generated code is not authored code

sites.why: drops any file sitting under a folder on the built-in list of generated and vendored trees
applies that built-in list before anything the project itself declares
prunes the same folders in the disk walk, so both ways of listing files give the same shape

rules.risk: Counting generated files inflates how big the project looks, which moves how many boxes the map is expected to have.

rules.statement: A project can name committed folders and files that the map is not meant to describe.
rules.name: Committed code can be declared out of the map

sites.why: tests each surviving file against the project's own exclusion list, kept separate from the built-in list
takes the file out of the analysed tree when the deciding pattern is an exclusion
a pattern naming a folder and no wildcard also covers everything beneath that folder

rules.risk: A fixture tree or a vendored copy would stay in the map forever. Version control is asked to commit those files, never to hide them.

rules.statement: When several exclusion patterns match one file, the last pattern written decides. So a later line can put one file back.
rules.name: The last pattern written decides

sites.why: keeps scanning after a match, so the answer is the last matching pattern and not the first
reads the file as excluded only when that deciding pattern is an exclusion, not a put-back
keeps the file when the deciding pattern is a put-back line

rules.risk: Without a later line winning, a broad exclusion could never be narrowed. One wanted file would then force the whole folder back in.

rules.statement: Every check and every screen reading a narrowed tree reports which patterns narrowed it and how many files went.
rules.name: A narrowed tree always says so

sites.why: the disclosure runs on every validate, before the coverage checks, not only in the expensive pass
the briefing shown before a build states how many files the project's own list removed
the pre-index report names the removed count and every pattern behind it
puts the note on the root of the file browser, so a narrowed tree is never shown as the whole project

rules.risk: The exclusion list is the one input able to hide a real gap from the checks that find gaps. Silence would make an incomplete map read as complete.

rules.statement: A pattern that removed no file is named on its own, including a line whose spelling can never match anything.
rules.name: A pattern that removed nothing is named

sites.why: collects the patterns that decided nothing, so no report can offer only a total
validate names those patterns in a warning of their own
the briefing before a build warns about them too
a line carrying a comment after the pattern is dropped and reported, because a comment only opens at the start of a line
a line made only of slashes is dropped and reported instead of being stored as a pattern that can never fire

rules.risk: A dead pattern reads as coverage the author never got. Hiding it inside a reassuring total is how a typo silently costs a coverage decision.

rules.statement: A measurement that moved too far asks for a human look, while a failed check stops the work.
rules.name: Drift asks, a failure stops

sites.why: any failed hard check makes the answer the blocking one, before anything else is considered
a breached allowance only reaches the softer answer, which asks for a person rather than blocking
the three answers leave three different exit codes, so an unattended run can tell them apart
the full run returns the same three codes, keeping the meaning identical wherever the comparison is invoked

rules.risk: Without the split, every normal wobble between two rebuilds reads as a failure, so real losses stop being believed.

rules.statement: A count that grew is never called worse, while a count that fell by thirty percent is.
rules.name: A finer map is never worse

sites.why: a shrink-only limit passes any growth and only breaches on a fall past the allowance
the name of each limit decides whether it is shrink-only or reacts to movement in both directions
sets the allowed fall for a raw count at thirty percent of the accepted map's count

rules.risk: A symmetric limit would call a map that found more parts a regression. The same limit would wave through a map that quietly lost half of them.

rules.statement: The number of boxes is measured against a count derived from the code, not against the accepted map.
rules.name: Zoom is judged against the code

sites.why: the expected number of boxes is computed fresh from the source tree at scoring time
the new map's distance is measured from that code-derived expectation, not from the accepted map
only the new map's distance decides the check; the accepted map's distance is shown but never decides

rules.risk: Judging zoom against the accepted map would lock its own wrong zoom into every map that follows it.

rules.statement: Judging that did not happen never becomes a score, for the map or against it.
rules.name: No score from judging that failed

sites.why: claims nobody could read are removed from the divisor, so they never lower the pass rate
a reader who says it could not reach the code is recorded as a failure, never as a disproof
a scoring stage that produced nothing yields no dimension scores instead of zeros
caps how much of the reading may fail before the whole reading is called untrustworthy
either side missing its reading breaches, so a skipped reading can never end in a clean pass

rules.risk: A failed reading counted as a disproof blames the map for a broken run. Counted as a pass, it hides that nothing was read.

rules.statement: A check that cannot run is reported as skipped, because silence would read as a check that passed.
rules.name: A skipped check says so

sites.why: the source-coverage check names itself as skipped when a map was scored without the code
a check that is always true against an older accepted map is announced as empty rather than reported as passing
the zoom check says it was skipped when the new map carries no code-derived expectation
the comparison of enforcement locations says it was skipped rather than reading absence as agreement
the scorecard refuses to score at all when the map cannot be read, rather than letting three map-reading rules score zero while the run still reports success

rules.risk: A quietly disabled check leaves the reader believing a whole class of loss was looked for and not found.

rules.statement: The run refuses a verdict when the map changed after freezing, or when the accepted map is missing.
rules.name: No verdict without the frozen map

sites.why: an empty freeze value is refused, so the guard is never switched off by an unnoticed typing mistake
refuses to score a map whose bytes no longer match the ones frozen when the run was picked
a named accepted map that is not there stops the run instead of quietly comparing nothing
an accepted map holding no scores stops the run, because an empty standard cannot produce a verdict

rules.risk: A run that compared nothing still reports success, so a later map is measured against a standard nobody ever set.

rules.statement: Judgements kept from an earlier run are thrown away when the judging method has changed since.
rules.name: Stored judgements die with the method

sites.why: a stored reading that does not record which judging method made it is treated as unusable
a stored reading made under a different judging method is refused, and the map must be judged again
two sides judged under different methods breach, so the comparison cannot end in a clean pass

rules.risk: Scores from two different judging methods are not comparable as one number. A change in the method then reads as a change in map quality.

rules.statement: The checkers are scored on how many deliberately false claims they refuse to confirm.
rules.name: The checkers are graded on planted lies

sites.why: confirming a claim that was made false on purpose is the only outcome scored as a miss
a moved code link counts as caught only when the checker reports a different line than the planted one
the four kinds of falsehood are planted in turn, so no single easy kind can dominate the score
a planted moved link must land on a real line of code, so the hard case is not quietly replaced by the easy one

rules.risk: Without a known answer, a low count of disproved claims cannot tell a good map from lazy checking.

rules.statement: A relationship, a step or a decision must name the code line that proves it, or the map is refused.
rules.name: No line, no claim

sites.why: refuses a relationship that gives no line and does not declare that none exists
refuses a decision that lists no place where it is enforced
refuses one enforcement place carrying neither a line nor a declared absence
refuses a step between two parts of the product that gives no line of its own

rules.risk: An unwitnessed claim cannot be checked. A wrong map then reads exactly like a right one.

rules.statement: A claim may declare that no single line enforces it. Declaring no line and naming a line at once is refused.
rules.name: A missing line is said out loud

sites.why: refuses an enforcement place that both declares no line and gives a line
warns when a relationship declares no line and still carries one
warns when a step declares no line and still carries one
leaves a declared absence out of the claim list a checker is asked to read

rules.risk: A blank left by accident and an absence chosen on purpose look identical. Nobody can then tell which claims were really read.

rules.statement: A code link must name one line, never a whole file. The line must exist in the file. A comment, a blank line or the opening line of a function cannot be the line that acts.
rules.name: One real line that can act

sites.why: refuses an enforcement place that names a file without a line
refuses the same file-only place while a worker is still writing its own rows
blocks a link whose file is not in the project
blocks a link naming a line past the end of the file
counts a blank line as a line that cannot act
matches the named line against shapes that never act, such as a comment or a function opening
runs that shape test over every link claiming an action fires there

rules.risk: A link nobody can open proves nothing. A link resting on a line that never runs proves nothing either, and it still looks grounded.

rules.statement: A relationship shows one example line where it happens. A step shows the exact line, which the reader can open. A change to that line hits the step it belongs to.
rules.name: An example, or the exact place

sites.why: shows exactly one line for each relationship, as a witness rather than a list of every call
renders a step's own line as a link the reader can open
registers a step's line, so a code change on it points back at that step

rules.risk: Reading a relationship's single line as the whole story hides every other place the same thing happens.

rules.statement: Two workers reporting the same relationship at the same line are folded into one claim. Two different lines are both kept, so a person decides which one is right.
rules.name: Same line, one claim

sites.why: makes the line part of what identifies a relationship, so only an exact match folds
keeps a relationship that names no line, because nothing tells two of them apart
flags one relationship declared twice at two different lines, for a person to settle

rules.risk: Folding two different lines together would silently throw away the one that was right.

rules.statement: A link found at the wrong line is reported, never taken as proof the claim is false. A reader may silence one report by writing down why the stored line is right.
rules.name: A moved link is a question, not a verdict

sites.why: sends every moved link out on the advisory channel, beside the other nudges
prints the moved-link count on a passing verdict, so a clean check still says how many moved
drops one report the reader has recorded as a false alarm
requires the whole claim and a non-empty reason, so one record answers one report
reports back a record that silences nothing, because the claim changed or the line was fixed

rules.risk: Failing a whole map over a moved link would throw away true claims. Hiding the report instead would let wrong lines pile up unseen.

rules.statement: Where a unit runs, how it is reached, and where a signal is emitted stay plain words. No single code line is that place.
rules.name: A place in the running system is not a link

sites.why: writes what a unit runs on and how it is reached as plain cells, with no link
writes where a signal is emitted and where it is watched as plain cells, with no link
shows the emit place in the browser as text, unlike the fields the viewer turns into links

rules.risk: Forcing a link here would make the author invent one. An invented link is worse than plain words.

rules.statement: A finding stops the work only when whoever receives it can still fix it. A judgement call only advises.
rules.name: Blocking only where a fix exists

sites.why: A disproved claim still standing in the map stops the run, because correcting or dropping it is always possible.
A code link pointing at the wrong line is only advice, because the repair tool cannot apply every one.
How boxes are grouped on a screen is recorded as information, and never allowed to move the verdict.
An access rule that names no stake stops the worker writing it, the one person able to answer.
A judgement-shaped nudge is printed for the worker and never fails the worker's own check.

rules.statement: A check that did not run never counts as a check that passed. The run names each check that was missing.
rules.name: Silence is not a pass

sites.why: One check that should have run and did not makes the whole verdict incomplete.
An incomplete read exits as a failure, exactly like a finding that blocks.
A fragment that could not be read gives a did-not-run verdict instead of a clean one.
A check this run could have done, and was not asked to do, is reported as its own line.
The written report lists every check that did not run, and says their silence is not a pass.

rules.statement: Closing a finding for good takes a written line that names the finding and gives the reason. A line that misses the name, or misses the reason, is refused.
rules.name: A reason, or nothing is recorded

sites.why: A line that names a finding and gives no reason is refused as a dismissal.
The one reader of these lines needs text after the separator before it reads a line as a record.
A heading no check reads is refused, because a line under it would silence nothing.
The batch is re-read after writing, and refused whole when one line answers no finding.
A stored line that tries to be a record and answers nothing is reported on every run.

rules.statement: A written reason answers only the findings it names. A line that would silence a whole family of findings silences none of them.
rules.name: One line answers one finding

sites.why: An unscoped deployment exception is reported as silencing nothing, because it once switched off every deployment finding at once.
A free-text key answers a line only when the line starts with that key, never when it merely contains it.
A recorded folder covers itself and what sits under it, never a neighbour whose name starts the same.
A key list holding one token that is not a key records nothing, rather than the part it could read.

rules.statement: A run always says what each written reason did. The count of findings that reason silenced is shown, or the fact that it silenced none.
rules.name: Every silence is reported

sites.why: Names how many deployment findings the written reasons swallowed, and which groups they covered.
Names the decision-sounding steps a written reason silenced, and says they were counted as done because of it.
Names a written reason silencing nothing today, so an inert line and a mistyped one are told apart.
Drops every written reason for one read, so a person sees the findings they hide without editing the map.

rules.statement: A map with open advice is never reported as clean. A run marks one piece of advice answered only where it can name the written line that answers it.
rules.name: Advice open is not clean

sites.why: Open advice gives the run its own verdict, which is not the clean one.
Says on screen that advice is not a pass, and that each piece is fixed or recorded.
Marks a piece of advice unanswered when the finding it names carries no recorded line.
Says the pairing cannot be decided, rather than guessing that a piece of advice was answered.

rules.statement: When two workers state the same thing differently, the merge stops and writes nothing. Neither version is quietly chosen over the other.
rules.name: The merge refuses to pick a winner

sites.why: Two workers claiming one identifier is a conflict, never one silently overwriting the other.
One fact stated twice with different values stops the merge, and both workers are named.
Two rows for one channel disagreeing on a value is reported, because the merge will not choose between them.
A merge conflict leaves no map written at all.

rules.statement: A folder of at most ten code files and three thousand lines counts as one box. A bigger folder is expected to hold several boxes instead.
rules.name: Where one box stops

sites.why: stops at a folder that fits both size limits and counts it as exactly one box
goes inside a folder that is over the limits, so its parts are counted one by one
counts an oversized folder with no sub-folders as several boxes, never as one

rules.risk: A box that quietly holds a whole subsystem cannot be opened. The reader sees one name where a dozen units live.

rules.statement: The expected number of boxes counts product code only. Documentation, configuration, tests, asset folders and nearly empty folders add no box to that number.
rules.name: Only product code raises the expected count

sites.why: drops documentation, settings and other text files before counting anything
drops test folders, internal folders and asset folders such as icons, images and translations
folds a nearly empty sub-folder into its parent rather than counting a box for it
counts the loose files of a folder as a box only when they hold real code

rules.risk: A project full of tiny pictures or settings files would be told to draw hundreds of boxes. Those boxes describe nothing about the product.

rules.statement: How coarse a map is can never fail a build, because every coarseness check only leaves a note. The note also stays quiet while the map sits within forty percent of the expected number of boxes.
rules.name: Coarseness advises, it never blocks

sites.why: files the box-count comparison under notes, never under failures
files the crowded-screen and thin-screen findings under notes, never under failures
says nothing at all while the number of boxes stays inside the forty percent margin

rules.risk: A guessed number with the power to block would force every map to the size a formula picked. The right size is the one that explains the product.

rules.statement: One screen reads well with three to nine boxes. Once a screen passes twelve boxes the map is told to group them.
rules.name: About five boxes to a screen

sites.why: counts a screen as reading well while it carries three to nine boxes
raises the crowding note when the first screen carries more than twelve boxes
raises the same crowding note when a group carries more than twelve boxes

rules.risk: A screen nobody can take in at one look is not a map. The reader is back to the file listing it was meant to replace.

rules.statement: A screen may stay crowded when its boxes are same-kind siblings sharing one folder or one name ending. Such a family is only called crowded above fifteen boxes.
rules.name: A family of look-alike boxes may be crowded

sites.why: reads the children as one family when two thirds of them sit in the same folder
reads the children as one family when two thirds of their names end in the same word
leaves such a family alone until it passes fifteen boxes

rules.risk: Cutting eleven look-alike boxes into invented groups adds a level that carries no meaning. The reader now clicks twice to read a list.

rules.statement: A thin screen is a fault on the first screen of a large map. Deeper in the map only a group holding exactly one box is called out.
rules.name: Where a thin screen is a fault

sites.why: raises the thin note when the first screen shows under three boxes and the map holds many
raises a note when a group holds exactly one box, so the level earns nothing
names the thin screens deeper in the map and states plainly that none of them is a fault

rules.risk: A first screen showing two boxes tells the reader which technologies are used. Nothing on it says what the product does.

rules.statement: A re-grouping suggestion may only move a box into another group. Merging two boxes into one, or cutting one box in two, is never suggested.
rules.name: Re-grouping moves boxes, never changes them

sites.why: starts from exactly the boxes already on the screen, so none is created and none is dropped
the only thing a suggestion adds to the map is a group row
the only change asked of an existing box is which group it belongs to

rules.risk: A suggestion allowed to merge or cut boxes to reach a nicer number changes what the map claims. The product's real shape is lost.

rules.statement: Each feature states by hand whether the product story must reach it. The map reports every feature whose claim the story contradicts. A feature that states nothing is reported too.
rules.name: A claimed place in the story

sites.why: reports a feature claiming the story must reach it, when no story step does
reports a story step whose work sits in a feature claiming the story skips it
separates a feature that answered nothing from a feature claiming the story skips it
rejects any answer outside the two allowed words, so an unanswered feature stays visible

rules.risk: Without the claim, the story can quietly drop main work or fill up with side work.

rules.statement: The party driving a use case is the one whose goal it serves. Machinery that only carries somebody's action inward is not a driver.
rules.name: The driver is the one with the goal

sites.why: blocks a use case that names no driving party at all
reports a use case naming a person and a program together, because the program is usually delivery machinery
reports a traced scenario whose opening party is not one of the declared drivers

rules.risk: A delivery mechanism counted as a driver puts a party in the story who wanted nothing.

rules.statement: Who a feature is for is never written on the feature itself. The people who drive it decide, and a program votes only when no person does. A feature that customers and the company's own staff both drive is flagged for a re-read.
rules.name: Who a feature is for, decided by its people

sites.why: sorts each driving party's vote by whether that party is a person or a program
counts the people's votes, and falls back to the programs only when no person voted
the feature's record takes the derived answer, so nothing on the feature can contradict its parties
reports a feature whose people pull to opposite sides, unless the map records why

rules.risk: A feature filed on the wrong side reads as customer work when only the company ever touches it.

rules.statement: A feature the walk never reaches still holds a place in the one story column. Its author names the feature it reads beside. Without that name the map guesses from the feature's own parties, and otherwise puts it last.
rules.name: Off the walk is not off the story

sites.why: uses the author's named neighbour when the feature carries one
falls back to the last walk step the feature's own parties drive
puts a feature with nothing to hang on at the end of the column
rejects a named neighbour that is not a defined feature
blocks a story place on a code area or a data area, because only a feature sits in the column

rules.risk: A feature dropped to the bottom reads as unimportant, which walk membership never said about it.

rules.statement: A front door is accounted for when a traced scenario reaches it, or a use case names it. A door nothing claims is reported, including one that starts itself with no caller. Writing a door off silences the report, and the map still counts it as a gap.
rules.name: Every front door answers to somebody

sites.why: lists every outside-facing door that neither a traced scenario nor a use case reaches
keeps a self-starting job in the same test, so having no caller is not an excuse
drops a door the map has written off, so the report stays quiet about it
counts the written-off doors out loud, so a silenced gap is still visible

rules.risk: An unclaimed front door is often a real capability nobody wrote down, and it stays hidden.

rules.statement: Every party that drives a feature states in its own words what it comes there to do. A blank line does not count as an answer. A line written for a party that drives nothing is reported too.
rules.name: Each party says why it comes

sites.why: reports a driving party that has no line of its own
blocks an empty line, which would count the party as covered while the arrow still falls back
reports a line written for a party that drives none of this feature's work
blocks these lines on a code area or a data area, because only a feature has parties coming to it

rules.risk: Without each party's own words, the picture labels every arrow with a catalog name.

rules.statement: When one person wears several roles, the map records the link between those roles. A role that turns into another names the action where the change happens.
rules.name: One person, several hats

sites.why: blocks a role change that names no action where the change happens
allows only two kinds of link, so a misspelled one cannot pass unseen

rules.risk: Without the link, the story draws one person as several strangers.

rules.statement: The map draws a kind of data only when the code defines it as a named type.
rules.name: No card without a real type

sites.why: rejects a data card that points at no definition in the code
requires that pointer to be a real file location, so a reader can open the type

rules.risk: Invented boxes fill the data picture with things a reader cannot open in the code.

rules.statement: The map credits a part of the project with owning data only when that part's own code writes it.
rules.name: Only the writer owns the data

sites.why: counts only save and write links when deciding which part owns a kind of data
turns an unclear touch into a read, so a filled-in link never grants ownership
raises a filled-in link to ownership only when some step shows a real write

rules.risk: A caller that merely asks for a save is named as the owner, so the real owner stays hidden.

rules.statement: Data that lives inside another record, in the source, or only during a call needs no owner.
rules.name: Data nothing writes needs no owner

sites.why: names the five ways of being stored that mean nothing in the project writes the data
excuses data stored in one of those ways from the missing-owner report

rules.risk: Every value object and short-lived shape is reported as a hole, so real missing owners drown in noise.

rules.statement: A save into a store must be explained by a named type that records the same store.
rules.name: Every save must name what it stores

sites.why: accepts the save when the saving part writes a named type kept in that store
also accepts it when the part saves on behalf of the type's owner, one step away

rules.risk: Real collections stay off the map because nobody gave the data a name, and the reader never learns they exist.

rules.statement: Where data lives must be recorded exactly enough for a reader to find it in the running system.
rules.name: Name the store, do not describe it

sites.why: flags a compartment named with no store linked to it
flags a compartment name that reads as a description, spotted by the space inside it

rules.risk: A described place cannot be looked up, so the reader cannot check the map against the real store.

rules.statement: A relation between two kinds of data is recorded on one side only, never twice.
rules.name: Each link between two types is written once

sites.why: rejects a pair where both kinds of data declare the same link
rejects the same link written twice on one card

rules.risk: The same link is drawn twice, and two copies that disagree leave the reader with no true version.

rules.statement: A lifecycle whose states no line declares is kept as a guess rather than thrown away.
rules.name: A lifecycle may be a guess

sites.why: marks a lifecycle citing no declaring line as guessed instead of rejecting it
makes the declaring line optional, with nothing written meaning guessed

rules.risk: Either real lifecycles vanish from the map, or a guessed one is read as proven.

rules.statement: A map is blocked when the numbers in its testing record contradict each other. Having tested very little only raises a warning.
rules.name: Contradiction blocks, thin testing only warns

sites.why: Blocks a record whose held-up, disproved and unsettled tallies do not sum to the number of statements checked.
Blocks a record claiming more statements were checked than the list ever held.
Blocks negative tallies, which can make a wrong record add up.
Sends those arithmetic failures to the blocking list, so a map cannot ship carrying them.
Sends every judgement about how much was checked to the warning list instead, so effort never blocks a map.
Warns when a map carries no testing record at all, so silence cannot read as a clean pass.
Warns when under three statements in five held up, and asks which statements were checked first.

rules.risk: The testing record is the only place a map says how much of itself was checked. Numbers that count nothing there make every other number look checked.

rules.statement: A check on one statement comes back held up, disproved, or impossible to settle from the code. A fourth answer is refused, never rounded into one of the three.
rules.name: Only three answers

sites.why: Refuses to write the record when any check carries a word outside the three answers.
Runs the same refusal the moment a checker returns, where the fix is still cheap.
Reaches the third answer only when a checker actually said the code cannot settle the statement.

rules.risk: Rounding an unknown answer into one of the three credits the map with a verdict nobody gave.

rules.statement: A statement counts as held up only when more than half of its checks agree. An even split is filed as unsettled and credited to neither side.
rules.name: A split vote settles nothing

sites.why: Requires a strict majority of the checks before a statement counts as held up.
Files an even split as unsettled rather than giving it to the larger-looking side.
Applies the same majority before the code-link check will touch a statement at all.
Lists a split apart from a checker's own cannot-settle answer, so a person adjudicates it.

rules.risk: Crediting a tie to one side turns a disagreement between checkers into a fact the map states.

rules.statement: A pass that left statements unchecked is refused until the operator declares that stopping early was deliberate. The declaration must name what was checked first.
rules.name: Stopping early must be declared

sites.why: Refuses the record while any statement has no verdict, unless the pass is declared partial.
Refuses the partial declaration when every statement did get a verdict, so a finished pass cannot understate itself.
Refuses a partial pass that carries no note saying which statements were checked first.

rules.risk: A pass that stopped early and a pass whose checkers died look identical from inside the tool. Without the declaration the map cannot say which happened.

rules.statement: How much of a map was checked is counted against the statement list as it stood before any fixes. Statements nobody voted on stay in that list.
rules.name: Scored against the list as it was pinned

sites.why: Refuses a verdict for a statement missing from the pinned list, which proves the wrong snapshot was used.
Keeps the whole pinned list as the total, so a short pass cannot shrink what it is measured against.
Subtracts an unvoted statement from the number checked, never from the total.
Counts separately how many statements the shipped map carries that a checker actually saw.

rules.risk: Counting against the fixed map shows nothing was ever disproved. The disproved statements are exactly the ones the fixes removed.

rules.statement: A statement the checkers disproved may not remain in the map word for word. A run that finds one fails.
rules.name: A disproved statement may not stay

sites.why: Fails the run when any disproved statement still matches the shipped map.
Names each disproved statement the map still carries word for word, which the counts alone cannot show.

rules.risk: The map would keep asserting something its own checkers proved wrong. Every count in the testing record would still read clean.

rules.statement: Correcting the code link under a statement never counts against the statement itself. The check that finds a moved link reports it and never fails a run.
rules.name: A moved code link is a correction, not a disproof

sites.why: Ends the code-link check as a report, so a moved link cannot block a map.
Skips statements whose link deliberately points at a definition rather than the acting line, so a different line is not a move.
Lets a person record for good that the stored link is the right one, so the finding stops repeating.

rules.risk: If a moved line read as a disproof, ordinary code moves would make a true map look wrong. The real defects would drown in the noise.

rules.statement: What coyodex does next is decided by the working tree, never by what the project's history still holds.
rules.name: The working tree decides the mode

sites.why: looks for an existing map only in the working tree, not in the project's history
refuses to restore a deleted map from history, so deleting it is how a person asks for a fresh build
stops and says the baseline is up to date when the code matches the pin, instead of writing an empty report
routes to change analysis when the code differs from the pin, uncommitted edits included

rules.risk: A person who deleted the map to start fresh gets the old map handed back instead.

rules.statement: Before any work starts, the person is told which files will be read and what the pin means.
rules.name: Briefing before any work

sites.why: requires the briefing to be the first message, shown word for word
prints the briefing: how many files will be read and what the map's commit will claim
names every ignore pattern that removed nothing, so a narrowing of the file set cannot pass unseen

rules.risk: Whole folders can be left out of the map, and nobody ever learns they were skipped.

rules.statement: A rebuild never opens the map it is replacing, so the new map cannot copy the old one.
rules.name: A rebuild never reads the old map

sites.why: forbids opening any earlier map during a build, filed archives included
warns when a map sits inside the set of files to be read, so a hand-made copy is not analyzed as source

rules.risk: Two maps that agree because one copied the other read as confirmation, and the old mistakes survive.

rules.statement: A map built on uncommitted code records a commit marked as not containing that code.
rules.name: Uncommitted code is pinned as uncommitted

sites.why: requires the marked pin whenever the person chooses to go on without committing
states, at the moment of the choice, that the marked pin means the code is in no commit
computes the pin and marks it whenever the tree holds uncommitted code
writes that same pin into the map's header, so the header cannot claim a clean commit

rules.risk: A pin that hides uncommitted code sends every later reader, and every later comparison, to the wrong lines.

rules.statement: Nothing the user owns is committed, stashed or overwritten unless the user asks for it.
rules.name: Nothing of the user's is changed unasked

sites.why: forbids committing or stashing the person's code, even to make the pin clean
repeats the same ban at the moment the pin is recorded
regenerates a map from scratch only on an explicit request, after a warning and a confirmation

rules.risk: A reviewed map, or a commit the person never intended, is lost, and coyodex cannot undo either.

rules.statement: Clearing the way for a rebuild files the old map away instead of deleting it.
rules.name: The old map is filed, never deleted

sites.why: moves each part of the map into the archive folder rather than removing it
puts back everything already moved when a move fails, so no half-filed map is left behind

rules.risk: A deleted map takes its recorded exceptions and corrections with it, and nothing can rebuild them.

rules.statement: A review of a build is refused while anything is still writing that build's map.
rules.name: No review of a running build

sites.why: refuses when any map file was written moments ago
refuses when another session has been active moments ago
refuses when the review would be reading the map its own session just wrote

rules.risk: A report about a half-written map describes a run that has not happened yet.

rules.statement: The map server answers only the person sitting at this machine. It listens on the loopback address and nowhere else. A request that names any other site is refused. A request that changes the remembered project list must carry a private marker header.
rules.name: Local machine only

sites.why: The server binds to the loopback address, so nothing off this machine can connect.
Every read request whose claimed site is not loopback is refused.
The same site check refuses a write request.
A write request without the private marker header is refused.

rules.risk: Without this limit, a web page open in the reader's browser could read the whole project's source code.

rules.statement: The server shows only project folders the user has opened before. It never searches the disk for maps. An address naming any other project is refused. A folder can be added only when it already holds a coyodex folder.
rules.name: Only folders you opened

sites.why: The served set is built from the remembered list alone, with no disk search.
An address that does not name a served project is refused.
Adding a folder is refused unless it holds a coyodex folder.
A folder named at startup is skipped under the same condition.

rules.risk: Without this limit, a page could name any folder on the machine and read the code inside it.

rules.statement: The code viewer opens a file only when it sits inside the project being shown. A path that climbs out of the project is refused. A link that points outside the project is refused too. From the working tree only files version control accounts for are served.
rules.name: Only in-project, tracked files

sites.why: An absolute or otherwise malformed path is rejected before any read.
A path containing a step up to the parent folder is rejected.
The code request refuses a bad path before touching disk or version control.
A working-tree read refuses anything inside the version-control folder.
The real resolved location must still sit inside the project, so a link cannot escape.
A file version control ignores is refused, so an ignored secrets file never leaks.

rules.risk: Without this limit, a reader could pull any file on the machine, including secrets kept out of version control.

rules.statement: What a reader sees always matches the map. Each file is read from version control at the commit the map was pinned to, not from the working copy. A map edited while the server runs is picked up on the next page load.
rules.name: Always the map's own version

sites.why: A code request defaults to the map's pinned commit; another version is asked for explicitly.
The file browser lists the files present at the map's pinned commit.
Every project request first checks whether the map changed on disk.
A changed map drops the stored copies of the browser tree, the views and the code symbols.

rules.risk: A reader trusting a code link would be shown lines that have moved. The map would look wrong where it is right.

rules.statement: The file browser never presents a shortened tree as the whole project. When the skip list hid files, the tree carries a note. The note says how many files went, which pattern removed each one, and which pattern removed nothing.
rules.name: A narrowed tree says so

sites.why: The note about what the skip list removed is attached to the top of the tree.

rules.statement: A link that leaves the page may open only a known code editor. The address must start with one of a fixed list of editor schemes. A hand-typed link template using any other scheme is refused.
rules.name: Editor links only

sites.why: An address outside the allowed editor list never becomes a clickable link.
Saving a custom link template is refused when its scheme is not on the list.

rules.risk: Without this limit a typed link template could run script inside the viewer. A reader could also be sent to an attacker's site.

rules.statement: The viewer page loads its two diagram libraries from the internet at exact pinned versions. Each one carries a fingerprint of the expected file. The browser refuses to run a file whose content does not match that fingerprint.
rules.name: Pinned outside libraries

sites.why: The pan and zoom library is pinned by fingerprint.
The diagram drawing library is pinned by fingerprint.

rules.risk: Without this check, a changed library file could run any code inside the viewer and read the project it shows.

extras.heading: Bucket vocabulary
extras.body:
Code parsing: the tree sizing needs a source parser, and no library seed names parsing
Testing & type checking: the test runner and the type checker are neither a framework nor a driver, and no seed names them
Build & packaging: the build backend is neither a framework nor a driver, and no seed names packaging
Coding agents: the skill installs into three AI agents, which share one real purpose no seed names
Code viewing: the browser, the hosting site and the editor share one purpose, which is showing the reader a file

extras.heading: Balance exceptions
extras.body:
store: coyodex writes plain files and depends on no datastore, so no entity can name one; each container is a file name
granularity: 31 components against a code-derived 19, because five of them are the written method and its two developer recipes, which are markdown and outside the count entirely; the remaining 26 follow real module seams
SF11, SF31: the lead prescribed both names in the shared sub-flow catalogue before running them past the naming check, and eight agents then referenced them; renaming mid-fan-out would have broken the contract, so the names stand and the mistake is recorded rather than tidied away
security-granularity: family — one rule per surface family, so a decision enforced at several endpoints is one rule with several sites; the loopback rule alone carries four sites across the bind, the host refusal and the write-path marker

extras.heading: Sweep debt
extras.body: eval/tools/coyodex_eval/process_scorecard.py:3160: prints each rule's before and after value and which way it moved; reporting a comparison is not a decision the product makes

extras.heading: Audit exceptions
extras.body:
read-before-create HP2: the briefing does not read an entry point; the command shell owns both the briefing and the whole command surface, so another flow's entry-point read leaks onto this step through one shared box
read-before-create HP5: a worker's self-check does read a testing record, because a testing record is an ordinary fragment; the record it reads belongs to an earlier build, not to the one the walk is describing
read-never-created HP17: a use case is written into the map by the fan-out workers at HP5, inside their own fragments, which the walk narrates as writing the whole map rather than each element type
read-never-created HP6: a component is written by the fan-out workers at HP5, inside their own fragments; the walk names the whole map at that step, never each element type it contains
read-never-created HP8: a group is assigned at HP7, which the walk narrates as writing the assignment file rather than as writing each group it names
why-less-step HP15: starting the map server is a second way into the story and needs nothing earlier; a reader may start it before any map exists and see an empty landing page
